Too = (i) to a degree exceeding normal or proper limits: The offer was too good to refuse. I was very tired but not too to go out. (ii) in addition; also; as well: She is young, intelligent, and rich too. He has a bike too. Can I come too? (iii) very: He didnt seem too interested for this job.

In a negative clause use either (NOT too/also/as well): The cheese cake was disappointing and the coffee wasnt very special either. (Compare: The food was excellent and the service was good too.)

Too + adjective + a/an +noun: Id accept the offer if I were you its too good an opportunity to miss.

Too many = more than is acceptable or required: I dont like television there are too many advertisements.

Too much + noun: I hope I havent caused you too much trouble.

Too + adjective/adverb (WITHOUT much): The dress was too expensive. If you speak too quickly, he doesnt understand.

`undefined` does not behave like a null though, it behaves much like `error` (it's basically `assert False`), it lets code typecheck but it will instantly throw an exception when executed.

It's usually used to stub code during development in TDD-type scenarios:

    myFunction = undefined

    myOtherFunction foo = doSomethingWith value
        where value = myFunction foo
will typecheck letting you fail your tests.

You can't have `undefined` "pass through" your code the way `null` does.

I'm not sure you can say that. `undefined` is a case of `error`, so it will blow up any time it's encountered (it's often used to stub code) not just when you try to use it, it's closer to putting a `throw` than to putting a `null`.
